{"batch":"item-briefs-2026-10-30-drain-2g","generated_at":"2026-10-30T12:00:00.000Z","authored_by":"session-lane","entries":[{"item_id":"947e08f3-0136-423d-8f62-03bb071bad49","source_pool_hash":"5322ca979d3bbd9f57b67aea3680f817dc264af6bf44a49920fc628654f7c1a0","body":"## 1. What the Research Found

The finding is a set of electricity forecasts from three held sources. The International Energy Agency (IEA) Renewables 2025 forecast says «Renewable electricity additions for 2025-2030 total 4 600 GW – equal to the combined installed power capacity of China, the European Union and Japan» The same forecast lowers its own earlier view: «Globally, we have lowered our renewable energy growth forecast for 2025-2030 by 5% compared to last year, to reflect policy, regulatory and market changes since October 2024. This revision means we now expect 248 GW less renewable capacity to be commissioned over 2025-2030.» For the United States it says «The US forecast is revised down by almost 50% across all technologies except geothermal.»

Two further held sources supplement the electricity picture. The U.S. Energy Information Administration Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) says «U.S. electricity demand in our forecast rises 1.3% in 2026, averaging almost 4,250 billion kilowatthours and growing another 3.1% in 2027.» The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) published its expert panel report on the Iberian blackout on «20 March 2026»; its press release says the factors «These factors led to fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections»

The page is stored only as a security-verification page and a 49-character title stub, and the source record shows one check, none successful, with the page last inaccessible on 2 May. No capture of the page or its PDF has been made, so no figure from either appears.

*Analytical inference:* the Renewables 2025 forecast and the STEO are forecasts, not outcomes; they say where capacity and demand are expected to go, not what any operator will pay. The ENTSO-E item is a post-event investigation, so its causes are findings about one event and not a forecast.

## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

*Analytical inference:* electricity cost and grid reliability sit under warehouse climate control, cold-chain facilities and the charging of ground-support equipment and road fleets.

On cost, the STEO says «Residential electricity prices are expected to increase by 5% in 2026 and to continue to rise in 2027, although at a slower pace.» It adds «Prices are rising across the United States, but the largest increases will likely occur in regions along the East Coast.» and «Electricity demand growth is led by growth in the commercial sector , which is expected to outpace residential demand in 2027 for the first time on record.»

The STEO overview table has the columns «2024 2025 2026 projected 2027 projected» and gives these rows: «Solar 5 7 8 9» «Natural gas 42 40 39 40» «U.S. CO2 emissions (million metric tons) 4,789 4,905 4,797 4,820»

*Analytical inference:* read across the columns, the U.S. CO2 total falls from 4,905 in 2025 to 4,797 in 2026 (the table's unit is million metric tons), the solar row rises (5, 7, 8, 9) and the natural gas row dips and recovers (42, 40, 39, 40). The consequence for a forwarder is a direction, not a factor: the table gives no grid emissions factor, so a facility's reported electricity emissions cannot be restated from it.

On reliability, ENTSO-E states that «developments at the local level can have system-wide implications»

*Operational implication:* the U.S. residential electricity price forecast is the only price the held sources give, and they give no commercial or industrial price; a forwarder with facilities in the U.S. East Coast corridor can read it as a direction for retail power cost, not as its facility tariff. For facilities in continental Spain and Portugal and the interconnected European system that the ENTSO-E report covers, the report documents a grid failure reaching beyond its origin. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by these sources.

## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

What the finding changes is the planning assumption behind renewable power procurement. The IEA reports that its main case «In our main case, recent cost trends, current policies and market developments raise cumulative renewable capacity to 9 530 GW in 2030 – a 2.6‑times increase from 2022.» The forecast adds «Nevertheless, the main case trajectory is not fully on track to triple global renewable capacity to around 11 500 GW, indicating that an ambition gap and implementation challenges continue to impede faster renewable power expansion.»

In its accelerated case the IEA «Conversely, our accelerated case assumes that governments address key policy, grid integration, financing and permitting challenges in the short term to unlock almost 20% more capacity growth compared with the main case. Under this case, cumulative renewable electricity capacity reaches over 10 400 GW, bridging most of the gap to global tripling by 2030.»

For China the IEA states that «While China’s 5% downward revision seems small in percentage terms, it is the second largest cut in absolute capacity (129 GW) following the United States.»

*Analytical inference:* a workspace that has promised clients abundant new renewable supply on a fixed timeline should test that promise against the IEA's own statement that its main case is not on track to triple capacity; a claim that the global tripling goal is being met is not supported by this source. The U.S. residential electricity price forecast and the demand forecast support a cost-planning direction for U.S. facilities, but the held sources give no commercial or industrial price; the IEA capacity figures do not support a price claim.

## 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

*Analytical inference:* what the workspace can credibly say is limited to what the held sources state. It can cite the IEA forecast as the source of the capacity direction and the STEO as the source of the U.S. price direction. A useful question to put to a client is which of its electricity assumptions rest on a published forecast and which rest on an expected connection date.

*Analytical inference:* a pitfall is to present a forecast as an outcome, or to cite the item's own Mid-Year Update figures, which this brief does not hold. Another pitfall is to read the ENTSO-E investigation as a verdict on renewable generation in general; the press release names many interacting factors.

## 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

What the finding does not resolve is the content of the item's own Mid-Year Update, whose figures are not held. The IEA Renewables 2025 page identifies its issuer as «IEA (2025), Renewables 2025 , IEA, Paris».

The held pages state no language on peer review or independent confirmation of the forecasts, so how settled the forecasts are is not stated.

The ENTSO-E recommendations are described only at a high level in the press release, so which of them change a facility operator's obligations is open. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any recommendation, once adopted into network codes, creates obligations for grid-connected logistics facilities.

- the captured STEO listed June 9, 2026 as its next release; that date has passed and no later STEO is held
- 2030: end of the IEA forecast period, with the main case at 2.6 times the 2022 level

The captured STEO page listed «Next Release Date: June 9, 2026» as its next release; that date has passed and no later STEO is held.
